1.overview: Ezekiel dates his vision by the River Kebar during the exile of King Jehoiachin and describes a storm cloud containing four living creatures. He then sees their accompanying wheels, an expanse and sapphire-like throne above them, and a humanlike figure surrounded by fire and brilliant light, whose appearance resembles the glory of the LORD.

sections.heading: The Throne and the Glory of the LORD

2.overview: The Spirit sets Ezekiel on his feet, and the Lord commissions him to speak to rebellious Israel whether the people listen or refuse, without fearing their opposition. The Lord tells Ezekiel not to rebel and gives him a scroll covered with words of lamentation, mourning, and woe.

3.overview: The LORD has Ezekiel eat the scroll and commissions him to speak to Israel, whose resistance he is equipped to withstand. The Spirit brings Ezekiel to the exiles at Tel-abib, where the LORD appoints him as a watchman and later confines him to his house, making his speech dependent on the LORD’s words.

4.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to portray Jerusalem under siege and to lie on his sides for assigned periods, bearing the iniquity of Israel and Judah. He prescribes meager, measured food and water for Ezekiel as a sign of Jerusalem’s coming famine, allowing cow dung instead of human excrement for baking the bread.

sections.heading: Ezekiel Bears Israel and Judah’s Iniquity

5.overview: The LORD commands Ezekiel to shave and divide his hair as a sign of Jerusalem’s coming destruction, with a few strands preserved and then burned. He condemns Jerusalem’s rebellion and defilement of the sanctuary, declaring judgments of famine, plague, sword, and scattering that will leave the city a ruin among the nations.

sections.heading: The Sign of the Divided Hair
The Terms and Effects of Judgment

6.overview: The LORD commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Israel’s mountains, announcing the destruction of its high places, altars, idols, and cities. He preserves a remnant scattered among the nations, while sword, famine, and plague bring judgment and leave the land desolate.

sections.heading: A Remnant Scattered Among the Nations
Judgment by Sword, Famine, and Plague

7.overview: Ezekiel announces that the end has come upon Israel, as the LORD brings judgment for the people’s ways and abominations. He describes violence, invasion, famine, plague, the loss of wealth and sanctuary, and the collapse of leadership, concluding that the people will know the LORD has judged them.

sections.heading: Survivors and the Loss of Wealth and Sanctuary

8.overview: Ezekiel is carried in a vision from the elders in exile to Jerusalem, where he sees the idol of jealousy at the temple and is shown Israel’s escalating acts of worship: elders honoring idols in secret, women weeping for Tammuz, and men worshiping the sun. God declares that Judah’s abominations and violence provoke his wrath, and that he will show no pity or hear the people’s cries.

9.overview: Ezekiel sees six armed executioners and a linen-clothed man summoned to the temple, where the LORD orders the man to mark those grieving Jerusalem’s abominations and the others to kill the unmarked, beginning at the sanctuary. Ezekiel pleads for Israel’s remnant, but the LORD cites the land’s bloodshed and the people’s claim that he does not see, declares that their deeds will fall on them, and receives the linen-clothed man’s report that he has obeyed.

sections.heading: The executioners arrive at the temple
The marked are spared; the killing begins
Ezekiel pleads and the man reports back

10.overview: Ezekiel sees the LORD’s glory above the cherubim and watches a man clothed in linen receive burning coals from among them. The vision describes the cherubim and their wheels as the glory moves from the temple threshold and the cherubim rise to the east gate.

sections.heading: The Glory Moves to the East Gate

11.overview: At Jerusalem’s eastern gate, the LORD condemns Jaazaniah, Pelatiah, and the other leaders for their counsel and violence, declares judgment on them, and Pelatiah dies as Ezekiel prophesies. The LORD promises to gather the exiles, give them a new heart and spirit, and judge the rebellious, while his glory leaves Jerusalem and Ezekiel returns to the exiles in Chaldea to report the vision.

12.overview: The LORD commands Ezekiel to act out an exile, then explains that the sign concerns Jerusalem’s prince and people: they will be taken captive, the prince will be caught and brought to Babylon, and a remnant will survive to testify among the nations. The LORD also portrays the fear and devastation awaiting Jerusalem and rejects sayings that visions fail or concern only the distant future, declaring that his words will be fulfilled without delay.

sections.heading: The prince and people taken captive

13.overview: The LORD commands Ezekiel to condemn Israel’s prophets for false visions and assurances of peace, and declares that they will be excluded from the people as Jerusalem’s whitewashed wall is torn down. He also condemns women who use charms and veils to deceive the people, promising to free those they ensnare and end their false visions and divination.

sections.heading: The Fall of the Whitewashed Wall
Judgment on the Women Who Prophesy

14.overview: Elders of Israel come to Ezekiel, and the LORD says that those who inquire while harboring idols will receive judgment, calling Israel to turn from its idols and declaring that inquirers and prophets share punishment. The LORD says that even the righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job cannot save others from famine, beasts, sword, or plague, but survivors from Jerusalem will be brought out as evidence of the city’s judgment.

sections.heading: Idolatry and inquiry before the prophet

15.overview: The LORD asks Ezekiel whether vine wood is more useful than other forest wood, and the answer is that it serves only as fuel and is useless once charred. The Lord GOD compares Jerusalem’s people to the vine, says he will set his face against them and give them to destruction, and declares that their unfaithfulness will leave the land desolate.

16.overview: The LORD recounts how he found Jerusalem abandoned, raised and adorned her, and made a covenant with her, but she trusted in her beauty, worshiped idols, and sacrificed her children. He announces judgment through her former lovers, compares her guilt with that of Samaria and Sodom, and promises to restore them and establish an everlasting covenant with Jerusalem.

sections.heading: Jerusalem’s origins and the LORD’s care
Judgment and comparison with her sisters

17.overview: The LORD gives Ezekiel a parable of two eagles and a vine, then explains that Babylon’s king takes Jerusalem’s king and establishes him under covenant, but the king turns to Egypt and breaks his oath. The LORD declares that the rebel will be captured and judged in Babylon, then promises to plant a cedar shoot on Israel’s heights, where it will flourish and display the LORD’s power to humble and exalt.

sections.heading: The Parable of the Eagles and Vine
The Parable Explained and Judgment Declared
The Cedar Shoot on Israel’s Heights

18.overview: The LORD rejects Israel’s sour-grapes proverb and declares that each person is accountable for their own conduct, illustrating the principle through a righteous man, his wicked son, and a grandson who acts righteously. He says the wicked who turn to justice will live and the righteous who turn to wrongdoing will die, then calls the house of Israel to turn from its transgressions because he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death.

sections.heading: A Call to Turn and Live

19.overview: Ezekiel is told to lament Israel’s princes through the image of a lioness whose first cub is taken to Egypt and whose second is captured by the nations and brought to Babylon. The lament then portrays Israel as a fruitful vine uprooted and dried by the east wind, with fire consuming its fruit and leaving no branch fit for a ruler’s scepter.

sections.heading: The First Lion Cub Taken to Egypt
The Second Lion Cub Taken to Babylon

20.overview: When Israel’s elders inquire of the LORD, Ezekiel recounts Israel’s repeated rebellion from Egypt through the wilderness and into the land, while the LORD withholds judgment for the sake of his name and promises to gather, judge, and restore his people. The LORD then announces fire against the forest of the Negev, and Ezekiel objects that the people dismiss his prophecy as a parable.

sections.heading: The elders’ inquiry and Israel in Egypt
Rebellion and judgment in the wilderness
Idolatry in the land and future restoration

21.overview: The LORD announces that His sword will strike Jerusalem and Israel, cutting off both righteous and wicked, and Ezekiel’s grief signifies the terror of the coming slaughter. The king of Babylon chooses Jerusalem by an omen, the prince of Israel loses his crown until the rightful ruler comes, and the Ammonites face judgment by the sword.

22.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to indict Jerusalem for bloodshed, idolatry, oppression, sexual offenses, and profanation, and announces that its people will be scattered among the nations. The LORD then portrays Israel as dross to be melted in Jerusalem and condemns the princes, priests, officials, prophets, and people for corruption, noting that no one stands in the gap before judgment falls.

sections.heading: Israel as Dross in the Furnace

23.overview: Ezekiel portrays Samaria and Jerusalem as the sisters Oholah and Oholibah, recounting Samaria’s pursuit of Assyria and Jerusalem’s pursuit of Assyria and Babylon before those powers turn against them. The LORD charges both cities with idolatry, child sacrifice, and profaning the sanctuary, and declares that judgment will expose and punish their sins.

sections.heading: Oholibah and the cup of judgment
Charges and judgment against both sisters

24.overview: Ezekiel dates the start of Babylon’s siege of Jerusalem and gives a boiling-pot parable portraying the city’s bloodshed, uncleanness, and coming judgment. After Ezekiel’s wife dies and he is forbidden to mourn, he explains that Jerusalem’s sanctuary and its people will fall, and that a fugitive’s arrival will end his silence and confirm his role as a sign.

sections.heading: The Boiling Pot and Jerusalem’s Judgment
The Fugitive and Ezekiel’s Open Mouth

25.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to announce judgment against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia for their contempt, claims, or hostility toward Israel and Judah. He describes each nation’s punishment and declares that they will know he is the LORD.

26.overview: Because Tyre rejoices over Jerusalem’s ruin and expects to profit, the LORD declares that many nations, beginning with Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, will destroy the city and its mainland settlements. The coastlands mourn Tyre’s fall, and the LORD declares that the city will become desolate, descend to the Pit, and never be found again.

27.overview: Ezekiel is commanded to lament Tyre, whose beauty and strength are depicted through a richly outfitted ship and an extensive trade network linking many lands. An east wind shatters the ship in the sea, sinking Tyre’s wealth and people as sailors and coastal nations mourn its downfall.

28.overview: Ezekiel declares judgment on Tyre’s ruler for claiming divine status, predicting his death at the hands of foreigners, and laments the king’s fall from splendor through pride, violence, and dishonest trade. He then prophesies judgment against Sidon and Israel’s restoration to its land, where the people will dwell securely.

sections.heading: Lament for the King of Tyre

29.overview: The LORD condemns Pharaoh and Egypt for claiming the Nile as their own and for failing Israel as a broken reed, declaring Egypt’s desolation and scattering for forty years before its restoration as a lowly kingdom. In a later oracle, the LORD gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment for his army’s labor against Tyre and promises a horn for Israel and speech for Ezekiel.

30.overview: The LORD announces the approaching Day of the LORD, when Egypt, its allies, and Cush face destruction, and names Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon as the agent who devastates Egypt and its cities. In a dated oracle, the LORD declares that Pharaoh’s arms will be broken, Babylon’s king will be strengthened against him, and the Egyptians will be scattered among the nations.

31.overview: In the eleventh year, the LORD tells Ezekiel to address Pharaoh and compares Assyria to a towering cedar nourished by abundant waters, sheltering nations and surpassing the trees of Eden. The LORD recounts Assyria’s cutting down and descent to Sheol as a warning of Pharaoh’s and Egypt’s coming downfall.

sections.heading: Descent to Sheol and Pharaoh’s fate

32.overview: Ezekiel delivers a lament for Pharaoh, depicting Egypt’s defeat by Babylon, its desolation, and the terror its downfall brings among the nations. In a second lament, Egypt descends to the Pit among slain nations including Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, and the leaders of the north, while Pharaoh finds comfort among the dead.

sections.heading: Pharaoh’s downfall and its cosmic signs

33.overview: The LORD appoints Ezekiel as a watchman for Israel, then declares that each person is judged according to whether they turn from righteousness or wickedness. After a fugitive reports Jerusalem’s fall, the LORD condemns the survivors’ claim to the land and says Ezekiel’s hearers listen to him without acting on his words.

sections.heading: Judgment According to Each Person’s Ways
Jerusalem’s Fall and the Land’s Judgment

34.overview: The LORD condemns Israel’s shepherds for exploiting and neglecting the flock, scattering the people, and announces that he will remove them and search for and restore his scattered sheep. He promises to judge between the sheep, appoint his servant David as their shepherd, and establish security, abundance, and a covenant of peace for Israel.

sections.heading: The LORD gathers and tends his flock
Judgment among the flock and David’s rule

35.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to prophesy against Mount Seir, declaring that its cities will be ruined and its land made desolate because Edom attacked Israel during its disaster. The LORD also condemns Edom’s claim to Israel’s lands and its contemptuous words and rejoicing over Israel’s desolation, promising judgment on Mount Seir and all Edom.

36.overview: The LORD promises the mountains of Israel fertility, resettlement, and freedom from the nations’ reproach, while declaring judgment against those who seized the land. He explains Israel’s exile as the result of its defilement and promises to gather, cleanse, and renew the people for the sake of his holy name, restoring the land and filling its cities with people.

sections.heading: Exile and the vindication of God’s name

37.overview: Ezekiel sees dry bones come to life through the LORD’s word and breath, and the LORD identifies them as the whole house of Israel, whom he promises to restore to their land. Ezekiel joins the sticks of Judah and Joseph, and the LORD promises to reunite Israel under one king, cleanse the people, and dwell among them forever.

sections.heading: The Dry Bones Come to Life
One King and an Everlasting Covenant

38.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, who gathers a multinational army and advances against Israel, a land whose people dwell securely. The LORD declares that Gog’s attack brings divine wrath and judgment, including earthquake, mutual slaughter, and calamities, through which he reveals his holiness to the nations.

39.overview: The LORD declares Gog’s defeat on the mountains of Israel, the destruction of his forces, and the cleansing of the land through the burning of weapons and burial of the dead. The nations recognize the LORD’s judgment, while Israel is restored from exile, gathered to its land, and assured that the LORD will no longer hide His face but will pour out His Spirit.

sections.heading: Gog’s Defeat and the LORD’s Name
Weapons Burned and the Dead Buried

40.overview: In a vision, Ezekiel is brought to a high mountain in Israel, where a bronze-like man measures the temple’s wall, courts, and gates. The man identifies the chambers and tables for priestly service and sacrifices, names the Zadokite priests, and measures the temple entrance.

41.overview: The man measures the outer and inner sanctuaries, the Most Holy Place, the surrounding side rooms, and the buildings and courts of the temple. He describes the wood paneling, carved cherubim and palm trees, the wooden altar, and the sanctuary doors and portico.

sections.heading: The Sanctuaries and Most Holy Place
The Side Rooms and Open Area
The Rear Building and Temple Interior

42.overview: The man leads Ezekiel through the north and south chamber buildings, describing their dimensions, levels, galleries, and entrances. He identifies the chambers as places for priests to handle and eat holy offerings and change garments, then measures the 500-cubit square boundary that separates the holy from the common.

sections.heading: Measured Boundary of the Temple Area

43.overview: Ezekiel sees the glory of the God of Israel enter the temple through the east gate and fill it, and hears God declare the temple his dwelling while calling Israel to abandon the practices that profaned his holy name. God instructs Ezekiel to describe the temple to Israel, gives the altar’s measurements, and sets out its purification and consecration rites for the priests of Zadok.

sections.heading: The Glory Returns to the Temple

44.overview: The LORD declares that the east gate remains shut because He entered through it, then rebukes Israel for defiling the sanctuary and assigns distinct duties to the Levites and the priests descended from Zadok. He sets out the priests’ clothing, conduct, teaching, judicial and purity duties, and provisions, declaring that the LORD is their inheritance.

sections.heading: Duties and Regulations for the Priests

45.overview: Ezekiel describes the holy district set apart for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, and city, with the prince’s land bordering it and the remaining tribal land protected from oppression. The chapter sets standards for fair measures and contributions, assigns the prince responsibility for offerings, and prescribes sanctuary purification and offerings for the Passover and seventh-month feast.

sections.heading: The Holy District and the Prince’s Land

46.overview: The LORD sets rules for the east gate, the prince’s and people’s worship, appointed offerings, and the prince’s handling of inheritances. Ezekiel is shown the priests’ chambers and the courts with kitchens where temple servants cook the people’s sacrifices.

47.overview: Ezekiel sees water flowing from the temple and growing into a river that freshens the Dead Sea, sustains abundant fish, and nourishes trees whose fruit and leaves provide food and healing, while marshes remain salty. The Lord GOD sets the boundaries for Israel’s land inheritance, assigns Joseph two portions, and includes resident foreigners and their children in the tribal allotments.

48.overview: Ezekiel describes the east-to-west land allotments for Israel’s tribes, with a central holy district for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, city, and prince. He names the city’s gates for the tribes and concludes that the city will be called “THE LORD IS THERE.”
